chapter: Studio craft and the TV and rock dates
title: Writers at sessions and the Tony Randall Show
summary: Sammy Nestico and Billy Byers ghost-write for the Tony Randall Show, with short bumpers that must be played in one take.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Were the writers and arrangers always at the sessions? © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

Kind of yes more so than not. Sometimes, like for instance I did the “Tony Randall Show” and the main writer was Pat Williams. But Pat wrote the theme song and then he would farm out to ghost writing with Sammy Nestico. And Sammy Nestico was the writer, the ghost writer for everybody out there. He and Billy Byers. Billy Byers was one of the most insane, greatest skilled writers I think I’ve ever seen in my life. Billy could sit and write a chart without a score, put it in his head, and he’d come back in 45 minutes and have a thing for you done. Billy was unbelievable. And Billy did stuff for Nelson Riddle and all these people you know. A lot of people out there got a lot of credit for shit they didn’t do, but when we did the “Tony Randall Show” Sammy was always there, because he did all of the inside charts, the little bumper things. You know when you’re doing television you do like an opening theme. At maximum it’s a minute and a half long or two minutes long. And then the closing theme where they put all the credits, that’s another minute and a half. You don’t play anything long. It’s all seven second, five second bumpers, scene changes you know[scats] that’s it. And you’d better be able to do that in one take because they don’t want to do those like seven times.
